diversity_guard.note: 5 distinct outlets, no outlet repeated; topics spread across research data, audiobook production, trade ethics/discourse, scholarly peer review, and detection tooling.

picks.title: What the Viral Study of AI in Self-Published Amazon Books Really Sets Out to Do
picks.excerpt: Tuhin Chakrabarty's peer-reviewed analysis of 14,419 self-published Amazon titles found signs of AI use in more than 25% of them. Those books sold less than human-written ones but still reached commercially viable revenue, complicating the assumption that readers simply reject AI-assisted work.
picks.rationale: First peer-reviewed numbers on how much of the Amazon self-publishing shelf is AI-assisted — and that it still sells — which resets the working assumption behind every AI-disclosure debate.

picks.title: HarperCollins is betting big on AI Audiobooks
picks.excerpt: HarperCollins is using its ElevenLabs partnership to push AI-generated narration into foreign-language editions and backlist titles that never justified a studio recording. The publisher says human narration stays its standard, while narrator groups warn about synthetic voices displacing professional voice work.
picks.rationale: A Big Five publisher naming exactly where synthetic narration gets used — backlist and translation — turns the AI-voice argument into a concrete production-budget decision.

picks.title: 'Hard to ignore' – AI speculation sparks debate about whether authors of colour targeted
picks.excerpt: A run of authors publicly suspected of using generative AI has triggered a trade-wide debate over whether writers of colour are disproportionately targeted by AI-detection speculation. Agents and publishers say unverifiable accusations are becoming a reputational risk with no reliable adjudication process.
picks.rationale: The cost of unverifiable AI accusations is landing unevenly, and the trade has no adjudication process — a governance gap anyone commissioning creative work now has to answer for.

picks.title: Guest Post — Do we need (r)evolution in peer review?
picks.excerpt: A guest post argues the peer-review system is buckling under reviewer shortages while AI reshapes both submissions and reports: AI-drafted manuscripts show measurably worse readability, and review reports increasingly look AI-assisted. It warns that only large publishers can afford AI reviewer assistants, widening the gap with smaller presses.
picks.rationale: AI is now on both sides of the review desk, and the tooling that copes with it is priced so only large publishers can buy it — a structural split worth watching before it hardens.

picks.title: Update on Substack's AI detection using Pangram
picks.excerpt: Substack's site-wide Pangram-based AI detection rollout has produced confusion and disputes among writers over false positives and opt-outs. A direct look at what happens when detection labels get attached to published prose by default.
picks.rationale: A major publishing platform is now labelling posts by detector score by default — the first place where false positives stop being theory and start attaching to your byline.
